summary.text: An alcohol is an organic compound that carries at least one hydroxyl (−OH) group bound to a saturated carbon atom.
The OH group strongly changes the properties of hydrocarbons, making them hydrophilic (water-attracted), and it gives a site where many reactions can occur.
Alcohols range from simple ones like methanol and ethanol to complex ones like sugar alcohols and cholesterol.

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: Arabic al-kuḥl, a powder used as an eyeliner

facts.label: Ethanol coined
facts.value: The term ethanol was invented in 1892

facts.label: Polyols
facts.value: Compounds with more than one hydroxy group

items.prompt: A molecule has an OH group attached to a carbon in an aromatic ring. Is it counted as an alcohol?

options.label: Yes, because any OH group on a carbon atom makes an alcohol
No, it is classed separately as a phenol with distinct properties
Yes, because the ring only adds to the molecule's size and shape
No, because an OH group can never attach to a ring carbon atom

items.explain: A hydroxy group bonded to an sp² carbon on an aromatic ring makes a phenol, which has distinct properties and is not classified as an alcohol.

items.prompt: Two alcohols share the same three-carbon chain, but one has its OH at the end and the other has it in the middle. How does systematic naming tell them apart?

options.label: A number between the alkane name and -ol gives the OH position
The middle one gets the prefix hydroxy- and the end one does not
The end one drops the -ol and takes an -al ending instead
Each gets a different Greek prefix for its carbon count

items.explain: The position of the hydroxyl group is shown by a number, as in propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol.

items.prompt: A compound has both an OH group and a carboxylic acid group. In its IUPAC name, how is the OH shown?

options.label: As the suffix -ol, since every OH group takes that ending
As the prefix methyl-, since the OH attaches to the chain
As the prefix hydroxy-, since the acid group takes priority
As the suffix -ol, with the acid shown as a prefix

items.explain: When a higher priority group such as a carboxylic acid is present, the prefix hydroxy- is used for the OH.

items.prompt: A label names a substance ending in -ol, such as cholesterol. What does that ending typically suggest about it?

options.label: It contains no oxygen at all
It is a metal-based powder
It is a fatty acid
It is an alcohol

items.explain: The suffix -ol in non-IUPAC names such as paracetamol or cholesterol also typically indicates that the substance is an alcohol.

items.prompt: Before it named a drinkable liquid, what did the word 'alcohol' originally refer to?

options.label: The flammable vapors that rise from boiling wine
A very fine powder made by heating the mineral stibnite
A cosmetic oil pressed from plants and spices
The salt that is added to wine before it is boiled

items.explain: The term was originally used for the very fine powder from sublimating stibnite, and its meaning was later extended to distilled substances and then narrowed to ethanol.

items.prompt: A chemist attaches an OH group to a hydrocarbon. What does that do to its relationship with water?

options.label: It becomes water-attracted
It becomes water-repelling
It becomes unable to react
It becomes a gas in water

items.explain: The OH group confers hydrophilic, water-attracted properties on hydrocarbons.

paragraphs.heading: What an alcohol is
paragraphs.text: An alcohol is an organic compound with at least one hydroxyl group, written −OH, attached to a saturated carbon atom. The family runs from small molecules such as methanol and ethanol up to bigger ones such as cholesterol and the sugar alcohols.

paragraphs.heading: Why the OH group matters
paragraphs.text: Putting an OH group on a hydrocarbon changes how that molecule behaves in a big way. It makes the molecule hydrophilic, which means drawn to water. The OH group is also a spot where many chemical reactions can take place.

paragraphs.heading: Naming alcohols
paragraphs.text: In official names set by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), the ending -ol marks an alcohol whenever the hydroxyl group is the highest-priority group in the molecule. For a simple alcohol, the final e of the alkane chain name is dropped and -ol is added, so ethane gives ethanol. A number can show where the hydroxyl sits: propan-1-ol is CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, while propan-2-ol is CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. Molecules with more than one hydroxy group are called polyols and take endings such as -diol and -triol, as in propane-1,2-diol, also known as propylene glycol.

paragraphs.heading: Primary, secondary and tertiary
paragraphs.text: Alcohols are sorted into primary, secondary and tertiary types. The sorting counts how many carbon atoms are joined to the carbon that holds the hydroxyl group, and in casual use the types are written 1°, 2° and 3°. Everyday names often pair the alkyl group with the word alcohol, as in methyl alcohol or ethyl alcohol. So the name propyl alcohol is ambiguous: it covers both n-propyl and isopropyl alcohol, which differ in whether the hydroxyl hangs off the end carbon or the middle carbon of the straight propane chain.

paragraphs.heading: Not every OH makes an alcohol
paragraphs.text: When the hydroxy group is bonded to a carbon in an aromatic ring, the molecule goes into a separate class called phenols. Phenols have properties of their own and are not counted as alcohols. Names can also hide the group: sugars such as glucose and sucrose carry hydroxyl groups, yet their common names have neither -ol nor hydroxy-.

paragraphs.heading: From eyeliner to ethanol
paragraphs.text: The word alcohol comes from the Arabic al-kuḥl, a powder worn as eyeliner. At first the term meant a very fine powder made by subliming the mineral stibnite, used as an antiseptic and a cosmetic as well as an eyeliner. Its meaning later widened to distilled substances in general and then narrowed to ethanol. In the 18th century it came to mean spirit of wine, and after 1850 chemists stretched it to the whole class now called alcohols.

paragraphs.heading: Distilling wine
paragraphs.text: Ancient thinkers such as Aristotle, Theophrastus and Pliny the Elder already knew that the vapors of wine could catch fire. A ninth-century writing attributed to Jābir ibn Ḥayyān noted that adding salt to boiling wine could make those vapors burn more readily. By the twelfth century, Latin recipes described making aqua ardens, or burning water, by distilling wine with salt. Taddeo Alderotti later described repeated fractional distillation through a water-cooled still that could reach 90% purity.
